newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - ISI approves NZ pension scheme progress.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - ISI approves NZ pension scheme progress.

text.p: The New Zealand Investment Savings and Insurance Association (ISI) is pleased with the way thinking is shaping up on the issue of compulsory superannuation, its chief executive said on Wednesday.

Roger Gill told Reuters in a telephone interview that nothing was yet set in concrete, but a speech in Wellington by Treasurer Winston Peters on Tuesday hinted that proposals for a compulsory retirement savings scheme were progressing along positive lines.

"There is still a fair way to go in the consultation process, but the picture is starting to get some shape and focus. We're broadly comfortable with the principles that (Peters) has indicated he is considering," Gill said.
He said the ISI was not in the business of arguing for or against compulsion, but wanted to ensure the scheme put to referendum in September was the best possible proposal.
A design team working on fine-tuning details of the scheme is due to publish its proposal in early June.
In a speech to the Association of Investment Advisers and Financial Planners in Wellington on Tuesday, Peters said the scheme was likely to be an annuity requiring at least NZ$160,000.

Once people saved more than the target amount they could stop saving, or take the extra savings as a lump sum. If they had saved less than the target, the amount could be topped up by the state, Peters suggested.
Gill said the ISI welcomed the suggestion that people would have no access to their savings until they retired, preventing them from borrowing against their account.
The ISI also saw as essential that contributors received their money through an annuity rather than in a lump sum.

"Investment restrictions was the other big thing (that had concerned the ISI) -- they're out, and there is no requirement that a certain percentage will need to be invested in New Zealand," Gill said.

He said normal prudential investment policy meant there would still be a degree of investment within New Zealand, but funds would also be spread offshore to get the diversification that gave good returns.
Gill said the ISI would not want to see any restriction on the types of assets people could invest in, other than the exclusion of very high risk, volatile assets.
"There are a lot of investment opportunities that are outside what you might call the mainstream...(that are) of a type that a reasonable person would go into knowing the risk profile."
Peters said the aim was to set up a regulatory regime that preserved the competitiveness of the market-based financial system.

Gill said the broadest, most flexible investment criteria, subject to the normal rules under the Trustee Amendment Act, should ensure fund managers covered their bases without focusing unduly on one particular asset type.
The lack of a formal government guarantee over people's savings was not seen by the ISI as a problem.

"Private sector fund managers will be competing for what potentially could be a considerable amount of money, so they've got to provide the returns and the results or they'll be towards the back of the queue when the choices are being made."

Gill said it was important the designers looked at the degree to which a compulsory savings scheme could be integrated with existing schemes to minimise the potential for distortion in financial markets. -- Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
